tip: Korean picks the wash verb by what you wash – 빨다 (ppalda) is only for fabric: 이불을 빨았어요 (ibureul pparasseoyo). Dishes and your body take different verbs.
놓아 주세요 (noa juseyo) ends in 주다 (juda = give) – adding it to a verb asks someone to do it as a favor for you: leave it at the door for me.
You don't 'take' photos in Korean – you 찍다 (jjikda), the snap-a-shot verb: 사진을 많이 찍었어요 (sajineul mani jjigeosseoyo) = took lots of photos.
-고 (-go) also links two states with no time order – 어지럽고 열도 나요 (eojireopgo yeoldo nayo) is just 'dizzy and feverish', not one thing then another.
후 (hu) = after and 전 (jeon) = before attach straight to nouns: 식후에 (sikhue) = after meals. Same pair as in 오전/오후 (ojeon/ohu = a.m./p.m.).
Korean splits tired: 졸려요 (jollyeoyo) = drowsy, ready to doze; 피곤해요 (pigonhaeyo) = worn out. Medicine makes you 졸려요 (jollyeoyo), the drowsy one.
Elders don't get plain 아프다 (apeuda = sick) – respect swaps in a whole different verb: 편찮으세요 (pyeonchaneuseyo) is how grandmother is unwell.
만들어 드렸어요 (mandeureo deuryeosseoyo) uses 드리다 (deurida), the humble 'give' for elders – with a friend the same favor would end in 줬어요 (jwosseoyo).
Korean describes how with sound-words: 눈이 펑펑 와요 (nuni peongpeong wayo) – 펑펑 (peongpeong) is fat snowflakes falling thick. Rain pours 주룩주룩 (jurukjuruk).
-기 시작하다 (-gi sijakhada) = start doing: 피기 시작했어요 (pigi sijakhaesseoyo) = started to bloom. The -기 (-gi) turns the verb into a noun the starting attaches to.
The sun 지다 (jida = sets) and 뜨다 (tteuda = rises) in Korean: 해가 일찍 져요 (haega iljjik jyeoyo) = the sun sets early. Same verbs work for the moon.
높아요 (nopayo) can end a sentence, but in front of a noun the adjective flips to -(으)ㄴ (-(eu)n): 높은 산 (nopeun san) = a high mountain.
보다 (boda = than) attaches to the thing you like less, and it comes first: 축구보다 야구를 (chukguboda yagureul) = baseball more than soccer – reverse of English order.
좋아해요 (joahaeyo = like) takes 을/를 (eul/reul): 영화를 좋아해요 (yeonghwareul joahaeyo). 좋아요 (joayo = is good) would need 이/가 (i/ga) instead.
'Good at games' takes a direct object in Korean: 게임을 잘해요 (geimeul jalhaeyo) – 잘하다 (jalhada) treats the skill as something you do to the game, no 'at'.
A -기 (-gi) phrase is a full noun and takes particles like one: 사진 찍기가 (sajin jjikgiga) puts the subject marker 가 (ga) right on 'photo-taking'.
Flat things get the counter 장 (jang) – photos, tickets, paper: 사진을 백 장 (sajineul baek jang) = a hundred photos, literally 'photos, hundred flat-things'.
보다 (boda) alone means 'than' – 더 (deo = more) just adds stress: 카메라보다 더 자주 (kameraboda deo jaju) = more often than the camera.
-(으)러 (-(eu)reo) + a motion verb = go somewhere to do it: 배우러 다녀요 (baeureo danyeoyo) = attend in order to learn. Only works with going-verbs like 가다 (gada).
'If' is an ending, not a word: -(으)면 (-(eu)myeon) glues onto the verb – 날씨가 좋으면 (nalssiga joeumyeon) = if the weather is good. No separate 'if' anywhere.
카톡 (katok) = KakaoTalk, Korea's default messenger – and it works as a verb: 카톡해요 (katokhaeyo) = text me. Brand names verbify freely with 하다 (hada).
쓰다 (sseuda) means both 'use' and 'write': 이모티콘을 써요 (imotikoneul sseoyo) = I use stickers. The same verb also writes letters and texts.
-아/어 놓다 (-a/eo nota) marks a state you set and leave in place: 무음으로 해 놓아요 (mueumeuro hae noayo) = set it to silent and keep it that way.
다 (da) before a verb means completely: 데이터를 다 썼어요 (deitareul da sseosseoyo) = used up all the data. Works anywhere – 다 먹었어요 (da meogeosseoyo) = ate it all.
다 됐어요 (da dwaesseoyo), literally 'has all become', is the everyday 'it died / ran out': 배터리가 다 됐어요 (baeteoriga da dwaesseoyo). Works for parking time too.
못 (mot) = can't, blocked or unable – different from 안 (an) = simply don't: 로그인을 못 했어요 (rogeineul mot haesseoyo) means the login failed, not that you skipped it.
꺼지다 (kkeojida) = turn off by itself; 끄다 (kkeuda) = turn it off. 갑자기 꺼졌어요 (gapjagi kkeojyeosseoyo) blames the phone – nobody switched it off.
Sound comes out on its own in Korean – 소리가 나다 (soriga nada = sound emerges). So 'no sound' is 소리가 안 나요 (soriga an nayo): the sound isn't coming out.
-비 (-bi) tacks 'fee' onto almost anything: 수리비가 (suribiga) = the repair cost, 택시비 (taeksibi) = taxi fare, 교통비 (gyotongbi) = transport costs.
-게 (-ge) turns an adjective into a how-word: 길다 (gilda = long) becomes 길게 눌러 주세요 (gilge nulleo juseyo) = press long, i.e. long-press.
때 (ttae) after a noun means 'at the time of': 세일 때 (seil ttae) = during the sale. No preposition needed – the noun plus 때 (ttae) does it all.
When the subject is someone honored, the verb takes -세요 (-seyo): 할머니는 좋아하세요 (halmeonineun joahaseyo) – grandma's verb gets the respect, not her name.
노트북 (noteubuk) looks like 'notebook' but means laptop – Konglish: 노트북을 샀어요 (noteubugeul sasseoyo) = bought a laptop. A paper notebook is 공책 (gongchaek).
켜지다 (kyeojida) = turn on by itself, the flip side of 켜다 (kyeoda = turn it on): 안 켜져요 (an kyeojyeoyo) = it won't come on, no matter who's pressing.
설날 (seollal) follows the lunar calendar – 음력 (eumnyeok) – so it lands in late January or February, never on January 1.
Koreans eat their age: 나이를 먹다 (naireul meokda) = get older, literally 'eat age'. 한 살 더 먹어요 (han sal deo meogeoyo) = eat one more year.
께 (kke) is the honorific 'to' – it replaces 에게 (ege) when the receiver deserves respect: 어른들께 (eoreundeulkke) = to the elders.
드리다 (deurida) is the humble 'give' aimed upward at elders – so the bow is offered: 정성껏 드려요 (jeongseongkkeot deuryeoyo). To a friend you'd 주다 (juda) instead.
The order is the ritual: 세배를 하고 (sebaereul hago = do the bow, and then) 세뱃돈을 받아요 (sebaetdoneul badayo) – the money only follows the bow, never before.
You can't state others' feelings directly – 기쁘다 (gippeuda = glad) becomes 기뻐하다 (gippeohada = show gladness) for other people: 아이들이 기뻐해요 (aideuri gippeohaeyo).
팔리다 (pallida) = get sold – it's 팔다 (palda = sell) with -리- (-ri-) making it happen to the tickets: 다 팔렸어요 (da pallyeosseoyo) = all sold out.
A number + -이나 (-ina) means 'that much?!': 다섯 시간이나 (daseot siganina) = a whole five hours. Drop it and the trip just took five hours, no eye-roll.
햇- (haet-) before a food means this year's first harvest: 햇곡식으로 (haetgoksigeuro) = with the new grain, 햇감자 (haetgamja) = new potatoes. One syllable marks freshness.
Dates always use Sino-Korean numbers: 오월 팔일 (owol paril) = May 8, literally 'five-month eight-day'. Native numbers like 다섯 (daseot) never touch dates.
달아 드려요 (dara deuryeoyo): -아/어 드리다 (deurida) turns an action into a humble favor for an elder – pin it on for them. With friends the ending is -아/어 주다 (juda).
